source: This C-terminal extension protrudes into the PpiB density, into which a high-resolution crystal structure of PpiB containing a bound substrate analogue (PDB: 1LOP; Konno et al., 1996) can be docked (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4f and citation (Konno et al., 1996).

claim: The resulting model strongly suggests that P68 from Abc2 would occupy the cis-trans isomerisation active site in PpiB.
source: The resulting model strongly suggests that P68 from Abc2 would occupy the cis-trans isomerisation active site in PpiB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural modeling shown in Figure 4f.

claim: A cis proline conformation at position 68 would disrupt the helical secondary structure and potentially direct the disordered C-terminus of Abc2 towards the RecB-RecC interface.
source: A cis proline conformation at this position would disrupt the helical secondary structure and potentially direct the disordered C-terminus of Abc2 towards the RecB-RecC interface.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from structural data.

claim: When the RecBCD-Abc2-PPI map is blurred and contoured down, a continuous weak density path can be observed for the continuation of the Abc2 C-terminus through the PpiB binding cleft and out towards the RecB helicase domains.
source: In fact, when the RecBCD-Abc2-PPI map is blurred and contoured down, a continuous weak density path can be observed for the continuation of the Abc2 C-terminus through the PpiB binding cleft and out towards the RecB helicase domains (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryoEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4c.

claim: Additional unaccountable patches of density are found above the noise in-between the 1A and 2A motor domains of RecB which enclose the ATP-binding site in the RecBCD-Abc2-PPI complex.
source: Looking around the RecB helicase domains, additional unaccountable patches of density are found above the noise in-between the 1A and 2A motor domains which enclose the ATP-binding site (Figure 4—figure supplement 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryoEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5a.

claim: The additional density near the RecB ATP-binding site is not seen in the Abc2 complex without bound PpiB.
source: This additional density is not seen in the Abc2 complex without bound PpiB (Figure 4—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryoEM data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5b.

claim: AlphaFold models of the Abc2 C-terminus are highly divergent and cannot be used to interpret the density.
source: AlphaFold (Yüksel et al., 2016) models of the Abc2 C-terminus are highly divergent and cannot be used to interpret the density (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of AlphaFold predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Low nanomolar concentrations of gp5.9 specifically inhibit RecBCD helicase activity in vitro by preventing DNA substrate binding.
source: In this work, we used biochemical and structural methods to study the interactions of two phage proteins, T7 gp5.9 and P22 Abc2, with the E. coli RecBCD complex. We found that low nanomolar concentrations of gp5.9 specifically inhibit RecBCD helicase activity in vitro by preventing DNA substrate binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of the RecBCD-gp5.9 complex explains the biochemical observations by showing how gp5.9 competes directly for the DNA binding site through mimicry of the natural DNA substrate.
source: Our structure of the RecBCD-gp5.9 complex explains the biochemical observations by showing how gp5.9 competes directly for the DNA binding site through mimicry of the natural DNA substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: T7 gp5.9 protein is functionally analogous to Gam from phage λ.
source: The T7 gp5.9 protein is functionally analogous to Gam from phage λ (Murphy, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Murphy, 2007) and comparison of functions.

claim: Both gp5.9 and Gam are small, dimeric, and highly acidic proteins which form a compact and predominantly alpha-helical structure.
source: Moreover, both are small, dimeric, and highly acidic proteins which form a compact and predominantly alpha-helical structure (Court et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Court et al., 2007) and structural data.

claim: The primary structures, overall folds, and the molecular-level details of the interaction of gp5.9 and Gam with RecBCD are different.
source: Despite these similarities, their primary structures, overall folds, and the molecular-level details of their interaction with RecBCD are different.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: DNA mimic proteins display a remarkable structural diversity.
source: Indeed, DNA mimic proteins display a remarkable structural diversity (Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: The coiled-coil architecture observed for gp5.9 has not been observed in nature before this study.
source: and, to the best of our knowledge, the coiled-coil architecture observed here for gp5.9 has not been observed in nature before this study.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of existing DNA mimic structures.

claim: The coiled-coil fold has been used previously as the structural framework for the rational design of synthetic DNA mimics targeting restriction endonucleases.
source: Interestingly, however, this fold has been used previously as the structural framework for the rational design of synthetic DNA mimics targeting restriction endonucleases (Yüksel et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Yüksel et al., 2016).

claim: This work validates the choice of coiled-coils for producing synthetic DNA mimic proteins.
source: Our work here validates the choice of coiled-coils for producing such synthetic proteins and may help inform their design against novel targets.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural findings.

claim: In cells containing the bacterial retron Ec48, the presence of either gp5.9 or Gam triggers programmed cell death as an abortive infection mechanism.
source: In cells containing the bacterial retron Ec48, the presence of either gp5.9 or Gam (either of which are indicative of phage infection) triggers programmed cell death as an abortive infection mechanism (Millman et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Millman et al., 2020).

claim: It was suggested that the retron binds directly to RecB and its release is triggered by Gam or gp5.9 to activate downstream effectors of cell suicide.
source: Because the Ec48 system is not tolerated in a ΔrecB mutant, and because Gam was known to bind mainly to RecB, it was suggested that the retron binds directly to RecB and its release is triggered by Gam or gp5.9 to activate downstream effectors of cell suicide by unknown mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Millman et al., 2020) and inference.

claim: The results are consistent with the hypothesis that Gam and gp5.9 bind to the same interface on RecB.
source: Our results here are consistent with this hypothesis because Gam and gp5.9 do indeed share the same binding location on the RecB arm domain and other nearby regions of RecB and RecC.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data.

claim: DNA, Gam, gp 5.9, and possibly the retron all compete for the same site on RecBCD.
source: Therefore, DNA, Gam, gp 5.9, and possibly the retron all compete for the same site on RecBCD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural data and prior knowledge.

claim: In retron-free E. coli cells, expression of gp5.9 likely sequesters all of the available RecBCD complex present at only ~10 copies per cell in an inactive form.
source: In retron-free E. coli cells, expression of gp5.9 likely sequesters all of the available RecBCD complex present at only ~10 copies per cell (Lepore et al., 2019; Taniguchi et al., 2010; Taylor and Smith, 1980) in an inactive form, thereby protecting T7 DNA from degradation and prioritising the use of phage-recombinases (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data and citations (Lepore et al., 2019; Taniguchi et al., 2010; Taylor and Smith, 1980).

claim: Gp5.9 may find use as a biotechnology tool for enhancing recombineering efficiency, improving cell-free transcription-translation systems, or stabilising DNA nanostructures in vivo.
source: In addition to its natural roles, gp5.9 may also find use as a biotechnology tool for enhancing recombineering efficiency, improving cell-free transcription-translation systems, or stabilising DNA nanostructures in vivo through its ability to potently inhibit RecBCD exonuclease activity (Sitaraman et al., 2004; Klocke et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations (Sitaraman et al., 2004; Klocke et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2000).

claim: The effects of Abc2 on RecBCD activity are complex and remain less well understood than is the case for the two DNA mimic proteins.
source: The effects of Abc2 on RecBCD activity are complex and remain less well understood than is the case for the two DNA mimic proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of understanding.

claim: Expression of Abc2 in E. coli eliminates RecBCD-dependent recombination but exonuclease activity is retained.
source: Expression of Abc2 in E. coli eliminates RecBCD-dependent recombination but exonuclease activity is retained (Murphy and Lewis, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Murphy and Lewis, 1993).

claim: There is no substantial effect of Abc2 on RecBCD helicase activity in vitro.
source: We found here that there is no substantial effect of Abc2 on RecBCD helicase activity in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previous biochemical studies showed that Abc2 had modest effects on RecBCD DNA binding (two- to fourfold tighter) and helicase-nuclease activity (three- to fourfold lower) in vitro.
source: Our results differ somewhat from previous biochemical studies (Poteete et al., 1988; Murphy, 1994; Murphy, 2000; Murphy, 2012; Murphy and Lewis, 1993) which showed that Abc2 had modest effects on RecBCD DNA binding (two- to fourfold tighter) and helicase-nuclease activity (three- to fourfold lower) in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Poteete et al., 1988; Murphy, 1994; Murphy, 2000; Murphy, 2012; Murphy and Lewis, 1993).

claim: It was shown that the RecBCD-Abc2 enzyme failed to respond to Chi and displayed properties that are somewhat akin to a constitutively Chi-activated complex.
source: Importantly, however, it was also shown that the enzyme failed to respond to Chi and displayed properties that are somewhat akin to a constitutively Chi-activated complex (upregulated 5′-exonuclease activity).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations in the surrounding text.

claim: Murphy and co-workers developed a model in which Abc2 hijacks RecBCD to generate the ssDNA required for phage recombination and modifies its RecA loading function to instead recruit its own recombinase (called Erf) to the ssDNA products.
source: Based upon their observations, Murphy and co-workers developed a model in which Abc2 hijacks RecBCD to generate the ssDNA required for phage recombination and modifies its RecA loading function to instead recruit its own recombinase (called Erf) to the ssDNA products (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and is a model/hypothesis.

claim: The biochemical and structural data are consistent with the hypothesis that Abc2 hijacks RecBCD.
source: Our biochemical and structural data are consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Abc2 is bound to RecC in close proximity to both a 'latch helix' which is thought to control conformational changes in response to Chi, and to an 'alternative exit channel' in the RecBCD complex.
source: Abc2 is bound to RecC in close proximity to both a 'latch helix' which is thought to control conformational changes in response to Chi, and to an 'alternative exit channel' in the RecBCD complex which is thought to accommodate a ssDNA loop in the post-Chi state (i.e. the recombinogenic mode) (Cheng et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2012; Handa et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and citations (Cheng et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2012; Handa et al., 2012).

claim: Under normal circumstances, the ssDNA loop would be loaded with E. coli RecA protein to promote subsequent steps in the host DNA break repair pathway.
source: Under normal circumstances, this loop would be loaded with E. coli RecA protein to promote subsequent steps in the host DNA break repair pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: It is plausible that Abc2 prevents RecA loading at the ssDNA loop site and/or promotes the binding of Erf to the emerging ssDNA.
source: Given its location, it is plausible that Abc2 prevents RecA loading at this site and/or promotes the binding of Erf to the emerging ssDNA, but this remains to be tested experimentally.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from structural data.

claim: The P22 recombination system includes the uncharacterised proteins Abc1 and Arf which are both required for full activity during P22 infection.
source: In addition to Abc2 and Erf, the P22 recombination system also includes the uncharacterised proteins Abc1 (Anti-RecBCD protein 1) and Arf (Accessory recombination factor) which are both required for full activity during P22 infection (Murphy, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Murphy, 2012).

claim: The role of Abc1 is unknown and its ability to bind directly to RecBCD has never been tested.
source: The role of Abc1 is unknown and its ability to bind directly to RecBCD has never been tested.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: The small size and acidic primary sequence of Arf hint that it might be a DNA mimic protein.
source: Likewise, exactly how Arf influences P22 recombination is unclear, but its small size and acidic primary sequence hint that it might be a DNA mimic protein.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from protein properties.

claim: The significance of the interaction between Abc2 and host PpiB is not clear.
source: Finally, the significance of the interaction between Abc2 and host PpiB is not clear.
evidence: The claim is based on the current state of knowledge.

claim: The structure shows that the PPI active site almost certainly engages P68 of Abc2.
source: Our structure shows that the PPI active site almost certainly engages P68 of Abc2
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data.

claim: It is plausible that proline isomerisation may in some way modulate Abc2 activity and therefore P22 infection.
source: and it is therefore plausible that proline isomerisation may in some way modulate Abc2 activity and therefore P22 infection.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from structural data.

claim: Proline isomerisation has been found to be critical for infection of E. coli by phage fd.
source: In this respect, it is interesting to note that proline isomerisation has been found to be critical for infection of E. coli by phage fd (Eckert et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Eckert et al., 2005).

claim: The RecBCD complex and related systems such as AddAB have been considered as attractive targets for antibacterial drug development.
source: The RecBCD complex and related systems such as AddAB (also known as RexAB) have been considered as attractive targets for antibacterial drug development (Lanyon-Hogg, 2021; Amundsen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Lanyon-Hogg, 2021; Amundsen et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of RecBCD/AddAB function reduces infectivity.
source: This reflects the fact that loss of RecBCD/AddAB function reduces infectivity (Gourley et al., 2017; Amundsen et al., 2008; Painter et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Gourley et al., 2017; Amundsen et al., 2008; Painter et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of RecBCD/AddAB function potentiates the effects of DNA-damaging agents.
source: potentiates the effects of DNA-damaging agents (Wilkinson et al., 2016b; Clarke et al., 2019; Clarke et al., 2021; Tamae et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Wilkinson et al., 2016b; Clarke et al., 2019; Clarke et al., 2021; Tamae et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of RecBCD/AddAB function reduces the potential for adaptive mutagenesis leading to antibacterial resistance.
source: and reduces the potential for adaptive mutagenesis leading to antibacterial resistance (Clarke et al., 2021; López et al., 2007; Bush et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Clarke et al., 2021; López et al., 2007; Bush et al., 2020).

claim: The diverse mechanisms employed by phage to manipulate bacterial DNA break repair may provide inspiration for the ongoing design of small-molecule inhibitors for RecBCD/AddAB.
source: The diverse mechanisms employed by phage to manipulate bacterial DNA break repair may provide inspiration for the ongoing design of small-molecule inhibitors for RecBCD/AddAB (Lanyon-Hogg, 2021; Lim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations (Lanyon-Hogg, 2021; Lim et al., 2019).
